claim: Fields as diverse as human genetics and sociology are increasingly using polygenic scores based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for phenotypic prediction.
source: Fields as diverse as human genetics and sociology are increasingly using polygenic scores based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for phenotypic prediction.
evidence: This is a general statement about current practice in multiple fields, drawing on established knowledge about the use of polygenic scores.

claim: Polygenic scores have limited portability across groups of different genetic ancestries.
source: However, recent work has shown that polygenic scores have limited portability across groups of different genetic ancestries, restricting the contexts in which they can be used reliably and potentially creating serious inequities in future clinical applications.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent work, indicating it draws from prior research.

claim: Within a single ancestry group (White British in UK Biobank), prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on socio-economic status of individuals.
source: Using the UK Biobank data, we demonstrate that even within a single ancestry group (i.e., when there are negligible differences in linkage disequilibrium or in causal alleles frequencies), the prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on characteristics such as the socio-economic status, age or sex of the individuals in which the GWAS and the prediction were conducted, as well as on the GWAS design.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the analyses shown in Figure 1.

claim: Within a single ancestry group (White British in UK Biobank), prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on age of individuals.
source: Using the UK Biobank data, we demonstrate that even within a single ancestry group (i.e., when there are negligible differences in linkage disequilibrium or in causal alleles frequencies), the prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on characteristics such as the socio-economic status, age or sex of the individuals in which the GWAS and the prediction were conducted, as well as on the GWAS design.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the analyses shown in Figure 1.

claim: Within a single ancestry group (White British in UK Biobank), prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on sex of individuals.
source: Using the UK Biobank data, we demonstrate that even within a single ancestry group (i.e., when there are negligible differences in linkage disequilibrium or in causal alleles frequencies), the prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on characteristics such as the socio-economic status, age or sex of the individuals in which the GWAS and the prediction were conducted, as well as on the GWAS design.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the analyses shown in Figure 1.

claim: Within a single ancestry group, prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on the GWAS design.
source: Using the UK Biobank data, we demonstrate that even within a single ancestry group (i.e., when there are negligible differences in linkage disequilibrium or in causal alleles frequencies), the prediction accuracy of polygenic scores can depend on characteristics such as the socio-economic status, age or sex of the individuals in which the GWAS and the prediction were conducted, as well as on the GWAS design.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the analyses comparing standard and sibling-based GWAS shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genetic architecture of human complex traits is almost always highly polygenic.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now been conducted for thousands of human complex traits, revealing that the genetic architecture is almost always highly polygenic, that is that the bulk of the heritable variation is due to thousands of genetic variants, each with tiny marginal effects (Boyle et al., 2017; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Boyle et al., 2017; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).

claim: The bulk of heritable variation in human complex traits is due to thousands of genetic variants, each with tiny marginal effects.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now been conducted for thousands of human complex traits, revealing that the genetic architecture is almost always highly polygenic, that is that the bulk of the heritable variation is due to thousands of genetic variants, each with tiny marginal effects (Boyle et al., 2017; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Boyle et al., 2017; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).

claim: Polygenic scores have been shown to help identify individuals at higher risk of breast cancer.
source: In human genetics, PGS have been shown to help identify individuals that are more likely to be at risk of diseases such as breast cancer and cardiovascular disease (Khera et al., 2018; Inouye et al., 2018; Mavaddat et al., 2019; Khera et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Khera et al., 2018; Inouye et al., 2018; Mavaddat et al., 2019; Khera et al., 2019).

claim: Polygenic scores have been shown to help identify individuals at higher risk of cardiovascular disease.
source: In human genetics, PGS have been shown to help identify individuals that are more likely to be at risk of diseases such as breast cancer and cardiovascular disease (Khera et al., 2018; Inouye et al., 2018; Mavaddat et al., 2019; Khera et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Khera et al., 2018; Inouye et al., 2018; Mavaddat et al., 2019; Khera et al., 2019).

claim: Papers have advocated that polygenic scores be adopted in designing clinical studies.
source: Based on these findings, a number of papers have advocated that PGS be adopted in designing clinical studies, and by clinicians as additional risk factors to consider in treating patients (Torkamani et al., 2018; Khera et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Torkamani et al., 2018; Khera et al., 2018).

claim: Papers have advocated that polygenic scores be used by clinicians as additional risk factors in treating patients.
source: Based on these findings, a number of papers have advocated that PGS be adopted in designing clinical studies, and by clinicians as additional risk factors to consider in treating patients (Torkamani et al., 2018; Khera et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Torkamani et al., 2018; Khera et al., 2018).

claim: Adaptation may often take the form of shifts in the optimum of a polygenic phenotype.
source: In human evolutionary genetics, several lines of evidence suggest that adaptation may often take the form of shifts in the optimum of a polygenic phenotype and hence act jointly on the many variants that influence the phenotype (Pritchard and Di Rienzo, 2010; Berg and Coop, 2014; Höllinger et al., 2019; Sella and Barton, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Pritchard and Di Rienzo, 2010; Berg and Coop, 2014; Höllinger et al., 2019; Sella and Barton, 2019).

claim: Polygenic scores are increasingly used in social sciences to distinguish environmental from genetic sources of variability.
source: Finally, in various disciplines of the social sciences, PGS are increasingly used to distinguish environmental from genetic sources of variability (Conley, 2016), as well as to understand how genetic variation among individuals may cause heterogeneous treatment effects when studying how an environmental influence (e.g., a schooling reform) affects an outcome (such as BMI) (Barcellos et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Conley, 2016; Barcellos et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2018).

claim: GWAS does not pinpoint causal variants, but instead implicates a set of possible causal variants in close physical proximity.
source: Notably, GWAS does not pinpoint causal variants, but instead implicates a set of possible causal variants that lie in close physical proximity in the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how GWAS works, supported by citations (Pritchard and Przeworski, 2001; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).

claim: The estimated effect of a SNP in GWAS depends on the extent of linkage disequilibrium with causal sites.
source: The estimated effect of a given SNP depends on the extent of linkage disequilibrium (LD) with the causal sites (Pritchard and Przeworski, 2001; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Pritchard and Przeworski, 2001; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).

claim: LD differences between populations lead to variation in estimated effect sizes and variable phenotypic prediction accuracies.
source: LD differences between populations that arose from their distinct demographic and recombination histories will lead to variation in the estimated effect sizes and hence to variable phenotypic prediction accuracies (Rosenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosenberg et al., 2019.

claim: About 80% of individuals included in current GWAS are of European ancestry.
source: In practice, given that most individuals (about 80%) included in current GWAS are of European ancestry (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016; Martin et al., 2019), PGS are systematically more predictive in European-ancestry individuals than among other people.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016; Martin et al., 2019).

claim: Polygenic scores are systematically more predictive in European-ancestry individuals than among other people.
source: In practice, given that most individuals (about 80%) included in current GWAS are of European ancestry (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016; Martin et al., 2019), PGS are systematically more predictive in European-ancestry individuals than among other people.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016; Martin et al., 2019) and logical inference from the fact that most GWAS are conducted in European-ancestry populations.

claim: Educational attainment of an individual depends on the genotypes of their parents due to nurturing effects.
source: For example, the educational attainment of an individual depends not only on their own genotype, but on the genotypes of their parents, due to nurturing effects (Kong et al., 2018), and of their peers, due to social genetic effects (Domingue et al., 2018), and of course on non-genetic factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2018.

claim: Educational attainment of an individual depends on the genotypes of their peers due to social genetic effects.
source: For example, the educational attainment of an individual depends not only on their own genotype, but on the genotypes of their parents, due to nurturing effects (Kong et al., 2018), and of their peers, due to social genetic effects (Domingue et al., 2018), and of course on non-genetic factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Domingue et al., 2018.

claim: Height shows strong patterns of assortative mating.
source: Also, traits such as height and educational attainment show strong patterns of assortative mating, which can distort effect size estimates in GWAS (Domingue et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017; Ruby et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Domingue et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017; Ruby et al., 2018).

claim: Educational attainment shows strong patterns of assortative mating.
source: Also, traits such as height and educational attainment show strong patterns of assortative mating, which can distort effect size estimates in GWAS (Domingue et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017; Ruby et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Domingue et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017; Ruby et al., 2018).

claim: Assortative mating can distort effect size estimates in GWAS.
source: Also, traits such as height and educational attainment show strong patterns of assortative mating, which can distort effect size estimates in GWAS (Domingue et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017; Ruby et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Domingue et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017; Ruby et al., 2018).

claim: Genotype-environment interactions are well-documented in other species, notably in experimental settings.
source: More generally, while we still know little about genotype-environment interactions (GxE) in humans, they are well-documented in other species—notably in experimental settings—and would further reduce the portability of PGS across environments (Gibson, 2008; Tropf et al., 2017; Mills and Rahal, 2019; Lynch and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Gibson, 2008; Tropf et al., 2017; Mills and Rahal, 2019; Lynch and Walsh, 1998).

claim: Genotype-environment interactions would reduce the portability of polygenic scores across environments.
source: More generally, while we still know little about genotype-environment interactions (GxE) in humans, they are well-documented in other species—notably in experimental settings—and would further reduce the portability of PGS across environments (Gibson, 2008; Tropf et al., 2017; Mills and Rahal, 2019; Lynch and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from established knowledge about GxE effects, supported by citations.

claim: Polygenic scores for some traits may include a component of environmental or cultural confounding with population structure.
source: PGS for some traits may also include a component of environmental or cultural confounding with population structure (Sohail et al., 2019; Haworth et al., 2019; Lawson et al., 2020; Kerminen et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2019); this source of confounding can increase or decrease prediction accuracy, depending on the structure in the prediction samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Sohail et al., 2019; Haworth et al., 2019; Lawson et al., 2020; Kerminen et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2019).

claim: The analysis focused on 337,536 unrelated individuals characterized as 'White British' in the UK Biobank.
source: To this end, we limited our analysis to the largest subset of individuals in the UKB with a relatively homogeneous ancestry: 337,536 unrelated individuals that were characterized by the UKB, based on self-reported ethnicities as well as genetic analysis, as 'White British' (WB) (Bycroft et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: The first 20 principal components of genotype data were used to adjust for population structure within White British individuals.
source: In all analyses, we further adjusted for the first 20 principal components of the genotype data, to account for population structure within this set of individuals (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Variation in diastolic blood pressure may arise for somewhat distinct reasons in males and females.
source: As a first case, we considered the prediction accuracy of a PGS for diastolic blood pressure in prediction sets stratified by sex, motivated by reports that variation in this trait may arise for somewhat distinct reasons in the two sexes (Reckelhoff, 2001; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Reckelhoff, 2001; Zhou et al., 2017).

claim: For diastolic blood pressure, when GWAS is conducted only in females, prediction accuracy is about 1.35-fold higher for females than for males.
source: When the GWAS is conducted only in females, the prediction accuracy is about 1.35-fold higher for females than for males; in turn, when GWAS was done in only males, the prediction accuracy in both sexes is similar, as well as somewhat decreased (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The qualitative trends in prediction accuracy differences across strata do not depend on the p-value threshold choice for SNP inclusion.
source: As we show, however, the qualitative trends reported in Figure 1 do not depend on the p-value threshold choice (Appendix 1—figure 3); moreover, the qualitative trends remain when LDpred is used (with a prior probability of 1 on loci being causal; Vilhjálmsson et al., 2015) instead of pruning approaches (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analyses presented in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The qualitative trends in prediction accuracy differences remain when LDpred is used instead of pruning approaches.
source: As we show, however, the qualitative trends reported in Figure 1 do not depend on the p-value threshold choice (Appendix 1—figure 3); moreover, the qualitative trends remain when LDpred is used (with a prior probability of 1 on loci being causal; Vilhjálmsson et al., 2015) instead of pruning approaches (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analyses presented in Appendix 1—figure 3, using a different methodological approach (LDpred).

claim: For the three example traits (diastolic blood pressure, BMI, years of schooling), prediction accuracies track SNP heritability differences across strata.
source: We first note that in these three examples, the prediction accuracies track SNP heritability differences across strata (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A, B, and C.

claim: For diastolic blood pressure, BMI, and years of schooling, estimated SNP heritabilities increase or remain the same with increasing phenotypic variance.
source: What we find instead is that the estimated SNP heritabilities for all three traits increase or remain the same with increasing phenotypic variance (Figure 2D,E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D, E, and F.

claim: For the three traits examined, variable prediction accuracy is not simply the result of differences in environmental heterogeneity across strata.
source: Thus, for these traits at least, the variable prediction accuracy is not simply the result of differences in the extent of environmental heterogeneity across strata.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing that heritability does not decrease with increasing phenotypic variance as would be expected if only environmental variance differed.

claim: Genetic correlations across strata for the three traits are close to 1 based on bivariate LD score regression.
source: This explanation is not supported by bivariate LD score regression, which indicates that the genetic correlations across strata are close to 1 (Appendix 1—table 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from bivariate LD score regression analysis presented in Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: When SNP effects are re-estimated in prediction sets, the estimated effects of trait-increasing alleles are larger in groups with higher prediction accuracy.
source: Yet when we re-estimate individual SNP effects in the prediction sets for SNPs ascertained in the original GWAS, the estimated effects of trait-increasing alleles are larger in the groups with higher prediction accuracy (Appendix 1—figure 4; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Using a linear mixed model (LMM) approach produces qualitatively similar results to using principal components for adjustment.
source: To examine this possibility, we repeated the analysis in Figure 1 but using a linear mixed model (LMM) approach (including PCs among other covariates; see Materials and methods), and obtained qualitatively similar results (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analyses presented in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Standard GWAS detects direct effects of genetic variants, but also indirect genetic effects of parents, siblings, or peers, effects of assortative mating, and potentially environmental differences associated with fine-scale population structure.
source: Standard GWAS is done in samples of individuals that deliberately exclude close relatives; as implemented, it detects direct effects of the genetic variants, but also any indirect genetic effects of parents, siblings, or peers, effects of assortative mating among parents, and potentially environmental differences associated with fine-scale population structure (Young et al., 2018; Trejo and Benjamin, 2019; Kong et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Young et al., 2018; Trejo and Benjamin, 2019; Kong et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2019).

claim: Many effects detected in standard GWAS are likely to be culturally mediated.
source: Given that many of these effects are likely to be culturally mediated (Stulp et al., 2017; Selzam et al., 2019), it seems plausible that they may vary within as well as across groups of individuals with different ancestries.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Stulp et al., 2017; Selzam et al., 2019) and logical inference.

claim: In sibling-based GWAS, genotype differences between siblings are tested for association with phenotypic differences, conditioning on parental genotypes.
source: In the latter, genotype differences between sibs, a result of random Mendelian segregation in the parents, are tested for association with the phenotypic differences between them. Because the tests depend on phenotypic differences between siblings who, of course, have the same parents, these tests are conditioned on the parental genotypes and hence exclude many of the indirect effects signals that may be picked up in standard GWAS (Appendix 1).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of sibling-based GWAS, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Sibling-based GWAS excludes many indirect effects signals that may be picked up in standard GWAS.
source: Because the tests depend on phenotypic differences between siblings who, of course, have the same parents, these tests are conditioned on the parental genotypes and hence exclude many of the indirect effects signals that may be picked up in standard GWAS (Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about how sibling-based GWAS works, with reference to additional explanation in Appendix 1.

claim: The UK Biobank contains approximately 22K sibling pairs, approximately 19K of whom are labeled as 'White British'.
source: A challenge in this comparison is that the UKB contains only ~22K sibling pairs, ~19K of whom are labeled as 'White British' (WB).
evidence: This describes the data available in the UK Biobank for sibling-based analyses.

claim: For the majority of traits examined, prediction accuracies of standard and sibling-based polygenic scores were similar.
source: For the majority of the traits, such as diastolic blood pressure, BMI, and hair color, the prediction accuracies of standard and sib-based PGS were similar (Figure 3B), as expected under standard GWAS assumptions and as observed for traits simulated under these assumptions (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and simulations in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: For height and a range of social and behavioral traits, the prediction accuracy of sibling-based polygenic scores was substantially lower than that of standard polygenic scores.
source: However, for height and for a range of social and behavioral traits, such as years of schooling, pack years of smoking and household income, the prediction accuracy of the sib-based PGS was substantially lower than that of the standard PGS (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: For height, standard and sibling-based polygenic scores perform similarly when based on the most significantly associated SNPs, but standard PGS progressively outperforms sibling-based PGS when more SNPs are included.
source: In contrast, for height, standard and sib-based PGS perform similarly when based on the most significantly associated SNPs, but standard PGS progressively outperforms sib-based PGS when more SNPs are included (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: For years of schooling, household income and other social and behavioral traits, the difference in prediction accuracy between sibling-based and standard polygenic scores changes markedly with p-value threshold.
source: Similarly, the difference in prediction accuracy between sib-based and standard PGS changes markedly for years of schooling, household income and other social and behavioral traits (Figure 3F and Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3F and Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: For hair color and diastolic blood pressure, there is little to no difference in prediction accuracy between standard and sibling-based estimation methods, regardless of the number of SNPs included.
source: For hair color and diastolic blood pressure, there is little to no difference in prediction accuracy between the two estimation methods, regardless of the number of SNPs included in the score (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The growing gap in performance between standard and sibling-based PGS with increasing p-value threshold likely reflects a combination of increasing noise-to-signal ratio and changes in the relative importance of direct effects versus other factors.
source: The growing gap in performance with increasing p-value threshold likely reflects a combination of an increasing noise-to-signal ratio for the effect estimates in sib-based versus standard GWAS (see Appendix 1) and changes in the relative importance of direct effects versus other factors such as indirect parental effects and assortative mating.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed data patterns and theoretical considerations discussed in Appendix 1.

claim: Differences between prediction accuracies of standard and sibling-based polygenic scores demonstrate that standard GWAS estimates often include a substantial contribution of factors other than direct effects.
source: In summary, the differences between the prediction accuracies of standard and sib-based PGS seen for a number of traits (Figure 3B), notably social and behavioral ones, demonstrate that standard GWAS estimates often include a substantial contribution of factors other than direct effects.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: When power to detect direct effects is comparable, standard GWAS would lead to higher prediction accuracy than sibling-GWAS for traits where standard GWAS includes substantial contributions from factors other than direct effects.
source: In these cases, even if the power to detect direct effects were comparable, standard GWAS would lead to higher prediction accuracy than sib-GWAS.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the observation that standard GWAS captures additional effects beyond direct genetic effects.

claim: The increased prediction accuracy from standard GWAS likely comes at a cost of not always porting well across groups, even of the same ancestry.
source: However, that gain stems from the inclusion of factors such as indirect effects and assortative mating that are likely to be modulated by SES, environment and culture (e.g., Selzam et al., 2019; Stulp et al., 2017). Thus, the increased prediction accuracy likely comes at a cost of not always porting well across groups, even of the same ancestry, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that factors contributing to higher prediction accuracy in standard GWAS are likely to vary across groups, supported by citations (Selzam et al., 2019; Stulp et al., 2017).

claim: Individuals in UK Biobank have higher SES than the rest of the British population.
source: For instance, individuals in UK Biobank have higher SES than the rest of the British population (Fry et al., 2017) and are presumably self-selected for a certain level of interest in biomedical research.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fry et al., 2017.

claim: UK Biobank participants are self-selected for a certain level of interest in biomedical research.
source: For instance, individuals in UK Biobank have higher SES than the rest of the British population (Fry et al., 2017) and are presumably self-selected for a certain level of interest in biomedical research.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the nature of opt-in biobank participation.

claim: The UK Biobank is a large study of about half a million United Kingdom residents, recruited between 2006 to 2010.
source: The UK Biobank (UKB) is a large study of about half a million United Kingdom residents, recruited between years 2006 to 2010 (Bycroft et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a factual description of the UK Biobank study, supported by citation to Bycroft et al., 2018.

claim: The UK Biobank collected hundreds of phenotypes through measurements and questionnaires at assessment centers and by accessing medical records.
source: In addition to genetic data, hundreds of phenotypes were collected through measurements and questionnaires at assessment centers, and by accessing medical records of the participants.
evidence: This is a factual description of the UK Biobank data collection, representing established knowledge about the study.

claim: The analysis focused on 408,434 participants who passed quality control measures provided by UK Biobank.
source: In this study, we focused on 408,434 participants who passed quality control (QC) measures provided by UKB; specifically, for whom the reported sex (QC parameter 'Submitted.Gender') matched their inferred sex from genotype data (QC parameter 'Inferred.Gender'); who were not identified as outliers based on heterozygosity and missing rate (QC parameter 'het.missing.outliers'==0); and did not have an excessive number of relatives in the database (QC parameter 'excess.relatives'==0).
evidence: This describes the data filtering and quality control procedures used in the study.

claim: Diastolic blood pressure levels were adjusted for blood pressure lowering medication by shifting values upward by 10 mmHg for individuals taking medication.
source: We adjusted the diastolic blood pressure levels for blood pressure lowering medication following Evangelou et al. (2018) by shifting the values upward by 10 mmHg for individuals taking medication.
evidence: This describes a methodological adjustment used in the study, following a procedure from Evangelou et al. (2018).

claim: UK Biobank participants were genotyped on either UK Biobank Axiom or UK BiLEVE arrays at a total of approximately 850K markers.
source: UKB participants were genotyped on either of two similar genotyping arrays, UK Biobank Axiom and UK BiLEVE arrays, at a total of ~850K markers.
evidence: This describes the genotyping platform used in the UK Biobank study.

claim: After filtering, 616,323 SNPs were used in the analysis.
source: We focused on autosomal bi-allelic SNPs shared between both arrays, and used plink v. 1.90b5 (Chang et al., 2015) to filter SNPs with calling rate >0.95, minor allele frequency >10−3, and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium test p-val >10−10 among the WB samples, resulting in 616,323 SNPs.
evidence: This describes the SNP filtering procedure and resulting dataset used in the study.

claim: 19,329 sibling pairs including 35,634 individuals across 17,328 families were identified among White British samples.
source: By this approach, we identified 19,329 sibling pairs including 35,634 individuals across 17,328 families.
evidence: This describes the sibling pairs identified in the UK Biobank data for sibling-based analyses.
